text: You already know Conditional Access requires MFA. At this stage the job is building policies that survive contact with a real tenant — understanding exactly how Entra ID evaluates them, and exactly how they fail.

Every policy is really four decisions. Assignments decide who and what — users or groups, cloud apps, and now workload identities as their own category. Conditions decide the context — sign-in risk, device platform, named locations, client app type. Grant controls decide what's required to get in — MFA, a compliant device, a hybrid-joined device, an approved app, or a flat block. Session controls decide what happens after sign-in, like sign-in frequency.

Here's what causes most production surprises: Entra ID doesn't pick one best-matching policy. Every policy whose assignments and conditions match gets evaluated, and all of their grant controls must be satisfied together. If one policy requires MFA and a separate one requires a compliant device for that same user, both apply at once. Design every new policy assuming it will stack with everything already in the tenant.

The most damaging failure mode is a policy that blocks the administrators who'd need to fix it. The defense is a break-glass emergency access account — cloud-only, Global Administrator, a long credential kept outside the tenant's normal control. The part people skip: that account must be explicitly excluded from every Conditional Access policy that could block it. If it isn't excluded, it isn't really a break-glass account.

Never flip a new policy straight to On. Build it in report-only mode first, which logs what would have happened without blocking anyone. Let it run against real sign-in patterns, then check the Conditional Access tab in the sign-in logs. For one specific scenario, the What If tool simulates a single sign-in against every policy in the tenant and shows exactly which would fire — before you ever switch a policy on for real.

Four decisions designed to stack safely, a break-glass account that's actually excluded, and report-only validation before enforcement — that's a policy built to hold up. Next lesson covers Privileged Identity Management, which makes those same admin roles time-boxed and just-in-time instead of standing and permanent.
